title: The computational universe
question: Does Wolfram's presentation of a computational universe give insufficient credit to Zuse's earlier proposal, as Schmidhuber argues?

usual_credit.summary: Stephen Wolfram's A New Kind of Science is associated with an extensive program studying simple computational rules and their possible relevance to fundamental physics. It should not be introduced as a standard historical consensus that Wolfram first proposed a computational universe, because his own historical notes mention both Zuse and Fredkin. [Independent commentary by Edwin Clark](http://shell.cas.usf.edu/~wclark/ANKOS_zuse_fredkin_thesis.html) also distinguishes the older cellular-automaton proposal from Wolfram's claimed approach. The credit disputed here concerns the novelty and presentation of the 2002 book, rather than an established physical discovery that the universe actually is a computer.

works.title: A New Kind of Science, Chapter 9 and historical notes on mechanistic models

claim.summary: Schmidhuber argues that Zuse had already proposed a discrete computational universe in 1967 and expanded the proposal in Rechnender Raum in 1969. He objects that Wolfram's historical note describes Zuse's idea as a continuous cellular automaton, which he considers a misleading distinction from Wolfram's own program. His criticism concerns attribution and novelty, not experimental proof that Zuse's physical hypothesis is correct.

prior_works.title: Rechnender Raum / Calculating Space (English technical translation, 1970)

quotes.text: Konrad Zuse who was the first to suggest that the physical universe is being computed on a discrete computer
as first suggested by computer pioneer Konrad Zuse in 1967

response.summary: No direct public reply from Wolfram to this specific criticism was located in the sources reviewed. His [2002 historical note](https://www.wolframscience.com/reference/notes/1026b/) does acknowledge Zuse and Fredkin but argues that literal mechanistic models are not the ultimate approach developed in the book. In an [independent discussion](http://shell.cas.usf.edu/~wclark/ANKOS_zuse_fredkin_thesis.html), mathematician Edwin Clark agrees that the cellular-automaton-universe idea did not originate with Wolfram, while pointing out that Wolfram's proposed ultimate models need not be classical cellular automata. That is a substantive distinction about what is claimed as new, although it does not settle whether the description of Zuse is accurate.

quotes.text: The idea that the universe may be a cellular automaton did not originate with Wolfram.
no such literal mechanistic model can ever in the end realistically be expected to work.

agreed_facts: Zuse's Rechnender Raum appeared as a book in 1969 and has a 1970 English translation: https://ncatlab.org/nlab/files/Zuse-CalculatingSpace.pdf
Wolfram's A New Kind of Science was published in 2002 and its historical note names Zuse and Fredkin: https://www.wolframscience.com/reference/notes/1026b/
Schmidhuber's online criticism identifies itself as based on a CERN Courier letter from June 2003: https://people.idsia.ch/~juergen/wolfram.html
crux: The issue is whether the computational-universe proposal and the scientific program presented by Wolfram are the same contribution, and whether his brief historical note fairly represents Zuse. An earlier speculation and a later program can share a broad idea without every model, method or novelty claim being identical.
